verses.text: There was a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year; and David sought the face of Yahweh. Yahweh said, “It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he put the Gibeonites to death.”

The king called the Gibeonites, and said to them (now the Gibeonites were not of the children of Israel, but of the remnant of the Amorites, and the children of Israel had sworn to them; and Saul sought to kill them in his zeal for the children of Israel and Judah);
and David said to the Gibeonites, “What should I do for you? And with what should I make atonement, that you may bless Yahweh’s inheritance?”

The Gibeonites said to him, “It is no matter of silver or gold between us and Saul, or his house; neither is it for us to put any man to death in Israel.” He said, “Whatever you say, that I will do for you.”
They said to the king, “The man who consumed us, and who devised against us, that we should be destroyed from remaining in any of the borders of Israel,
let seven men of his sons be delivered to us, and we will hang them up to Yahweh in Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of Yahweh.” The king said, “I will give them.”
But the king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan the son of Saul, because of Yahweh’s oath that was between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul.

But the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bore to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite.

He delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the mountain before Yahweh, and all seven of them fell together. They were put to death in the days of harvest, in the first days, at the beginning of barley harvest.

Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water poured on them from the sky. She allowed neither the birds of the sky to rest on them by day, nor the animals of the field by night.
David was told what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done.

So David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son from the men of Jabesh Gilead, who had stolen them from the street of Beth Shan, where the Philistines had hanged them, in the day that the Philistines killed Saul in Gilboa;
and he brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son. They also gathered the bones of those who were hanged.

They buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son in the country of Benjamin in Zela, in the tomb of Kish his father: and they performed all that the king commanded. After that, God answered prayer for the land.
The Philistines had war again with Israel; and David went down, and his servants with him, and fought against the Philistines. David grew faint;
and Ishbibenob, who was of the sons of the giant, the weight of whose spear was three hundred shekels of brass in weight, he being armed with a new sword, thought he would kill David.

But Abishai the son of Zeruiah helped him, and struck the Philistine, and killed him. Then the men of David swore to him, saying, “Don’t go out with us to battle any more, so that you don’t quench the lamp of Israel.”
After this, that there was again war with the Philistines at Gob. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, who was of the sons of the giant.
There was again war with the Philistines at Gob; and Elhanan the son of Jaare-Oregim the Bethlehemite killed Goliath the Gittite’s brother, the staff of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam.
There was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on every hand, and six toes on every foot, twenty four in count; and he also was born to the giant.
When he defied Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimei, David’s brother, killed him.
These four were born to the giant in Gath; and they fell by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants.

footnotes.content: Three years of famine—what a long dark stretch. David finally asks the Lord why, and the answer cuts deep: his predecessor's violence toward the Gibeonites echoes still. Sometimes our famines aren't puzzles to solve but debts to acknowledge. The Lord makes us look back before He lifts His hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Gibeonites were not Israel by blood, yet bound by oath—they were under Israel's protection by covenant. Saul broke faith and broke law, nursing zealotry into bloodshed. I've learned: a good cause doesn't justify breaking your word. The Lord will not overlook it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David doesn't hide from the wrong or make excuses—he looks the harmed people in the eye and asks what restitution looks like. That's the heart of a king whom the Lord can work with. He seeks not their favor but their blessing, their reconciliation with the God of Israel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice how the Gibeonites refuse silver—they don't want blood money or to play judge themselves. They want justice under God, not revenge in private. David's promise is blank: 'Whatever you say.' That's humility: when you've inherited an old debt, you don't haggle about terms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Gibeonites name their wound plainly: 'a man who consumed us.' Saul tried to erase them from the earth. That's no small matter—it's genocide attempted. Even now, long after Saul's death, the wound hasn't healed. Speaking our hurts to God's anointed is how reconciliation begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven men of Saul's house—the number of completion, of justice done. And they ask David to hang them 'before Yahweh' at Gibeah, Saul's own stronghold. It's not revenge; it's restitution made public and before God. David agrees. Some wrongs require that kind of visibility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But David protects Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, because of the oath between him and Jonathan. Not all of Saul's house will fall—love and covenant work forward too. Even in executing justice, David remembers the friend he loved. Grace and truth stand together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rizpah's two sons, Michal's five—not one of them had chosen to persecute the Gibeonites, yet they bear their father's guilt. It's a hard truth: we inherit the consequences of the ones we love. But their deaths do atone; their sacrifice quiets the land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven men hanged 'before Yahweh'—the phrase shows this is not murder but a solemn, witnessed act before God. They fall together at harvest time, when the land should be yielding bread, not blood. Yet sometimes the Lord requires such things to break a curse and let grace flow again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rizpah spreads sackcloth on the rock and keeps vigil from harvest through the rains—weeks of weeping, watching over the bodies of her sons. A mother's grief becomes a witness to God. She guards the dead as only love can. Who grieves for those we lose? Who stands guard?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Word reaches David: Rizpah has been keeping her vigil. The king hears of a mother's faithful love for her dead, and that witness moves him. Sometimes the Lord speaks through the grief of others to stir the king's heart toward mercy and remembrance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David goes to Jabesh Gilead to retrieve Saul's bones—an act of honor he didn't owe to his rival. Even ancient enemies deserve a grave. Saul's bones had hung in Beth Shan, dishonored; now David restores them. In doing so, he shows that even old conflicts find their rest in burial.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They gather not only Saul and Jonathan, but also the bones of the seven who were hanged—the very ones who died for the curse, now brought together to be buried with honor. Restitution and remembrance merge. The dead are given rest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kish's tomb holds Saul and Jonathan once more, and the seven rest near them. David obeys fully, and then—then—'God answered prayer for the land.' The curse breaks. A three-year famine ends because a king made restitution, a people grieved, and the dead were honored. That's how the Lord moves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: War returns—the Philistines press again. David goes out with his men, but age is catching him; his strength flags. A king who has loved well, grieved well, and made peace with the past—and now faces a new trial. The battles don't end. But neither does the Lord's care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ishbibenob—a giant's son, three-hundred-shekel spear, new sword—comes hungry to kill the aging king. In that moment, David is vulnerable. Sometimes the giants don't come when we're young and strong; they wait for our weariness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But Abishai strikes first. David's men cry out: 'You are the lamp of Israel—don't risk yourself.' What a thing to be told. A man isn't meant to burn forever; but while his light shines, it mustn't be snuffed out early. Love and wisdom say: this is not your time to die.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sibbecai kills Saph at Gob—another giant falls. The battles blur together in old age, but each victory is real. The Lord's hand is on His people, working through faithful servants, one battle after another.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elhanan kills Goliath's brother—yes, the same spear-shaft like a weaver's beam, the giant's bloodline still reaching across generations. The victory over Goliath echoes here too, but it's others now who stand in the breach. The Lord's people continue the work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man at Gath with six fingers, six toes—twenty-four in count, born of the giant's line. How strangely sin marks the world—deformity, excess, a living reminder that rebellion against God leaves its strange signature in creation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan son of Shimei—David's brother—kills him. Another name we'll never know much about, doing his part when the moment came. The Lord uses many hands. Not all of His warriors get songs written. Some just show up and strike true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four giants born to Gath's line, all fallen—by David's hand, by his servants' hands. Readers today hear an echo: the battles the Lord wins aren't fought alone. He raises up servants, ordinary faithful people, to do His work across generations. Our part may be small, but it's real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
